title: National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015
short_title: National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would change the main law governing the national vocational education and training regulator.
It aims to protect the VET system's integrity, reduce regulatory burdens on training organisations, and improve how the regulator operates.
The changes include extending registration periods and requiring clearer marketing of VET courses, with no significant financial cost expected.
changes: Extend the period for which training organisations can be registered.
Require clearer marketing of vocational education and training courses.
Make administrative amendments to clarify existing provisions.
summary.affected: Registered training organisations and the Australian Skills Quality Authority are affected.

divisions.question: Christopher Pyne I would like to thank members who have contributed to this debate. The Australian government's focus on skills is working to restore trades and vocational education and training to their rightful place at the centre of our national economy. Ensuring Australian workers are highly skilled and job-ready is critical to national economic growth and productivity and a key plank of the government's industry innovation and competitiveness agenda. The Australian government has embarked on significant VET reform, which has included widespread consultation. Our reforms are focused on ensuring vocational education and training is led by industry and employer needs. They are also focused on ensuring the national VET system delivers quality training that has the confidence of students, employers and the wider community. The National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 strengthens the regulation of registered training providers and third-party brokers in order to address quality concerns. The bill amends the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Act 2011 and introduces measures to protect the integrity of the national training system to provide better balance in the regulation of the training system and to improve the efficiency and operation of the act and consequently the national regulator, the Australian Skills Quality Authority, known as ASQA. In particular, extending the maximum period of registration for registered training providers from five to seven years will enable the ASQA to focus its compliance efforts on those doing the wrong thing rather than on registration or renewal audits, which providers expect and prepare for. The introduction of a quality standard-making power sends a clear signal to all in the training sector that, when required, the Commonwealth government will quickly take action against those who undermine the quality of training provided to students or abuse taxpayer funding. Sharon Bird by leave—I move amendments (1) and (2), as circulated in my name, together: (1) Schedule 1, item 6, page 6 (lines 4 and 5), omit the item, substitute: 6 Subsection 17(5) Omit "more than 5 years", substitute: more than: (a) 5 years; or (b) if the application is to renew the registration of an NVR registered training organisation that the Regulator has rated as low risk (using the Risk Assessment Framework)—7 years. (2) Schedule 2, item 2, page 16 (line 11), omit "registration, including renewal of registration", substitute "renewal of registration". The opportunity to discuss these matters in the previous debate on the second reading of the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 gave me the opportunity to outline the reason that Labor has put this amendment forward in the consideration in detail section—and I just want to reiterate it in the few minutes in this part of the debate. I indicated that Labor recognises that the vast bulk of this bill is intended to provide really sensible amendments to the powers of the regulator and the government in order to increase or improve definitional terms—for example, as many members indicated, the fact that the original bill's RTO strict definition was hampering and tying the hands of the regulator with respect to some of those purported RTO activities that were going on in the market—and to provide some significant quality assurance improvements, particularly the ability for the minister to act more speedily to address some of the things that had emerged in the market. We absolutely endorse many of those. The message from those amendments is particularly important and useful for the general public at the moment—and that is why I commend the government for them. speeches.speaker: Melissa Price
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, arguing that it would improve quality, accountability and administration by enabling new standards, clarifying responsibility for marketed courses, extending RTO registration from five to seven years, and strengthening action against poor-performing providers. Reported that Western Australia had 164,000 public VET students in 2013 and $199 million in government funding.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, including stronger marketing transparency, quality standards and registration periods of five to seven years. Reported that the government had committed $68 million over four years to ASQA, that 23 RTO audits were planned, and that trade support loans provided up to $8,000 in the first year and up to $20,000 over four years.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: Supported amendments to the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, arguing that it needed stronger consumer protection against providers and brokers leaving vulnerable students with debts and no useful qualifications. Called for an ACCC information campaign, an Auditor-General audit of VET FEE-HELP, and extending registration from five to seven years only for existing low-risk providers.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, arguing that it would improve quality, transparency and enforcement while reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens. Reported that the government would provide almost $6 billion this year for VET, had committed $68 million over four years to ASQA, and would extend registration periods from five to seven years for providers that complied with requirements.

speeches.speaker: Nick Champion
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 while calling for ACCC consumer protection measures and an Auditor-General audit of VET FEE-HELP, citing constituent Lukus Whitehead whose diploma loan debt rose to $30,000.

speeches.speaker: Nickolas Varvaris
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, arguing that it would improve enforcement, course transparency and protection from poor-quality providers. Reported that retirees were projected to increase from one supported by five working adults to one supported by 2.7 working adults by 2050, and said the bill would extend registration from five years to seven years and support a national complaints hotline.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 and proposed further protections for students affected by poor-quality providers. Reported that VET businesses had made super-profits of 30 per cent and that Victoria's TAFE share had fallen from 70 per cent to 20 per cent, and called for registration extensions to apply only to low-risk providers and for an ACCC campaign.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Scott
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, describing rogue registered training organisations that sign up vulnerable students to costly courses, and cited New South Wales's 564,000 vocational education students and the government's $579 million subsidy to keep courses affordable.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Argued that unscrupulous vocational education providers are exploiting vulnerable students, citing a constituent's $16,787.97 debt to Careers Australia, and criticised the government's skills funding cuts and New South Wales's Smart and Skilled TAFE privatisation policy.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 with the member for Cunningham's amendments, and criticised Evocca College for enrolling 38,000 diploma students while only 2,000 graduated, leaving people such as Dylan Palmer with large VET FEE-HELP debts.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 to protect students from unscrupulous training providers, recounting his own 1974 apprenticeship earning $39 a week and welcoming trade support loans of up to $8,000 in the first year and $20,000 over four years for apprentices such as his son.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 but urged stronger consumer protections, citing misleading practices, VET FEE-HELP debts, and concerns about TAFE funding, fees, courses, and access in New South Wales.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: Supported the bill as an improvement to vocational education regulation but argued it did not go far enough to address harm to vulnerable students, VET FEE-HELP exploitation, declining course quality, reduced TAFE funding and inadequate student support.

speeches.speaker: Kelvin Thomson
speeches.brief: Supported the bill and amendment, arguing that unscrupulous RTOs and brokers had left vulnerable students with large debts and poor or no qualifications, and calling for stronger oversight, consumer protection and action to ensure vocational training leads to employment.

speeches.speaker: Ewen Jones
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, arguing that ASQA needs stronger powers to address poor-quality and unscrupulous providers while reducing burdens on consistently high-performing organisations; the bill would add $68 million in funding and extend registration from five to seven years.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 and its second-reading amendment, arguing for transparency, ethical marketing and stronger protection of students from predatory providers, VET FEE-HELP debts and unsuitable courses; also called for an ACCC consumer protection campaign.

speeches.speaker: Sharman Stone
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, arguing that new quality standards and stronger ASQA oversight would address unscrupulous providers, poor courses and damage to TAFE; the bill would extend registration from five to seven years and target high-risk providers.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 while seeking amendments to protect students from unscrupulous providers and brokers, including tighter conditions for extending registration from five to seven years; cited VET FEE-HELP debts, $97,728 access limits, $1.6 billion allocated last year and a 40 per cent non-repayment estimate.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, reporting concerns about vulnerable people being recruited into unsuitable courses and debts through cash inducements, iPads and laptops; said the bill would strengthen quality standards, broker accountability and ASQA investigations, supported by $68 million over four years.

speeches.speaker: Brendan O'Connor
speeches.brief: Supported the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015, arguing that stronger oversight and accountability were needed to protect students from unscrupulous providers, brokers and large VET FEE-HELP debts, including debts often around $20,000 and access of up to $97,728.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Thanked members for debating the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 and argued it strengthens regulation of training providers and brokers by extending maximum registration from five to seven years, introducing a quality standard-making power for the regulator ASQA, and tightening marketing transparency requirements.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Bird
speeches.brief: Moved amendments to the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment Bill 2015 so a seven-year registration period would apply only on renewal for training providers the regulator rates low risk under its Risk Assessment Framework rather than to all providers, citing scandalous behaviour and student debts in the VET market.
